subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: Which statement about alkanes is accurate?

options.text: They contain alternating single and double bonds within a closed ring
They contain at least one carbon–carbon double bond and follow the formula CnH2n
They contain a carbon–carbon triple bond and follow the formula CnH2n−2
They contain only carbon–carbon single bonds and follow the formula CnH2n+2

explanation:
Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons: every carbon–carbon bond is a single bond, so each carbon holds the maximum possible number of hydrogens, giving CnH2n+2. Propane (n = 3) therefore has 2(3) + 2 = 8 hydrogens. The other choices define alkenes (CnH2n), alkynes (CnH2n−2), and aromatic rings such as benzene, all of which are unsaturated because a pi bond or ring reduces the hydrogen count.

ELI-10: Each carbon must form four bonds. In an alkane, a carbon spends only one bond on each neighbor, so every leftover bond goes to a hydrogen and the molecule carries as much hydrogen as it structurally can, which is what saturated means. Check it with propane: 2(3) + 2 = 8 hydrogens, matching C3H8 on a propane tank label. This same counting rule is why saturated dietary fats have no double bonds while unsaturated fats do.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
